article.headline: A Painted Census of God's Warning Signs, Rediscovered After Centuries
article.lede: The *Augsburger Wunderzeichenbuch* — the **Augsburg Book of Miracles** — is a lavishly illuminated manuscript of 169 pages assembled in Augsburg, Germany, around 1545–1552: a painted compendium of every extraordinary thing God had apparently sent to warn or instruct humanity. One of the most visually arresting documents of the Reformation era, the book spent roughly four and a half centuries lost to scholarship before resurfacing at a European auction in 2008. A Taschen facsimile edition, published in 2013, returned it to wide attention.
article.body:
The manuscript is executed entirely in *gouache* and watercolour on paper, each of its 169 pages rendered at large format — 21.5 by 33 centimetres — with some pages heightened with gold. The German captions follow Martin Luther's 1545 Bible translation, firmly placing the work in Protestant intellectual culture. Its patron and original commissioner remain unknown. The book's two identified artists are Hans Burgkmair the Younger, son of the famous Augsburg master, and **Heinrich Vogtherr the Younger** (1513–1568), who trained under his father Heinrich Vogtherr the Elder, a major figure in Reformation printmaking. Vogtherr the Younger spent his most productive years in Augsburg between roughly 1540 and 1554 — precisely the manuscript's production window — before relocating to Vienna. The 2025 *Hollstein* catalogue raisonné of his prints, the standard scholarly reference for his graphic output, runs to 302 pages; he is the less well-documented of the two hands, and the *Wunderzeichenbuch* is among his most significant surviving attributions.

The illustrations range across three grand domains. The first fifteen folios retell Old Testament miracles — Moses parting the Red Sea with figures dressed in contemporary Augsburg clothing, Jonah and the whale, the visions of Ezekiel. A vast central section documents nearly 160 non-biblical wonders from antiquity to 1552, including what scholars describe as probably the largest early collection of comet pictures: twenty-six blazing comets rendered in brilliant yellows and gold. The section also includes *parhelia* — the optical phenomenon of multiple simultaneous suns formed when sunlight refracts through airborne ice crystals — along with celestial cavalry battles, volcanic eruptions, blood rains, and hybrid monstrous creatures. The final nineteen surviving folios depict the *Book of Revelation*'s apocalyptic beasts and cataclysms. The sequence closes on a hailstorm over the Dutch city of Dordrecht on 17 May 1552 — the manuscript's last dated wonder, and the key to establishing when it was completed.

This was the culture of *Wunderzeichen* — **wonder-signs** — the German Reformation's mass-media genre of divine portent. Nearly four hundred broadsheets and tracts recording celestial and terrestrial wonders were published across German-speaking lands between 1550 and 1599 alone. Lutheran theology supplied the interpretive frame: Philip Melanchthon asked, "if these signs are not meant to be considered, why are they written and painted on the sky by divine providence?" Comets, eclipses, and monstrous births were read as evidence that the Final Judgment was imminent and the Pope was the Antichrist. What distinguishes the *Wunderzeichenbuch* within the genre — as the critic Marina Warner observed in the *New York Review of Books* in 2014 — is the near-total absence of moralising commentary. The images are presented as visual spectacle, with captions recording each wonder without insisting on its lesson. For a book made in the midst of Reformation polemics, the restraint is striking.

After the sixteenth century the manuscript's provenance is entirely obscure. Rebound in the nineteenth century, it disappeared from all scholarly record. In 2008 it resurfaced at auction in Europe and was acquired by the American collector Mickey Cartin. Taschen published a scholarly facsimile in 2013 — two volumes in a clamshell box — with commentary by curators Till-Holger Borchert and Joshua P. Waterman; a smaller-format second edition followed in 2017. In 2021 David Zwirner gallery in New York mounted the first substantial public exhibition of original folios. Warner called the manuscript "a gorgeous unheralded surprise: a foundling of unknown parents, a virgin birth." Four and a half centuries after it was made, it has finally found its audience.

concepts.definition: German for 'wonder-signs': extraordinary natural or supernatural phenomena — comets, parhelia, monstrous births, atmospheric visions — interpreted in Reformation-era Germany as messages from God. The genre encompassed illustrated broadsheets, pamphlets, sermons, and painted compendiums, and was closely tied to Lutheran eschatology and apocalyptic expectation about the imminence of the Final Judgment.

An opaque water-based paint made by mixing pigment with water and a binding agent such as gum arabic, with chalk or white pigment added to produce opacity rather than translucency. Unlike transparent watercolour, gouache yields dense, matte areas of colour well-suited to manuscript illumination and the kind of flat, legible illustration found in the Wunderzeichenbuch.

An atmospheric optical phenomenon — also called 'mock suns' or 'sun dogs' — in which bright spots of light appear to the left and right of the sun, caused by sunlight refracting through hexagonal plate-shaped ice crystals suspended in the atmosphere. Medieval and early modern observers frequently interpreted parhelia as divine portents; the Wunderzeichenbuch records at least a dozen separate occurrences.

A comprehensive scholarly catalogue of all known authenticated works by a given artist, typically including provenance, condition, exhibition history, and bibliography for each entry. The *Hollstein* series — volumes of which cover Vogtherr the Younger's prints — is the standard catalogue raisonné for early Netherlandish and German graphic art.

books.title: Augsburger Wunderzeichenbuch (Augsburg Book of Miracles)
books.author: Anonymous (attributed to Heinrich Vogtherr the Younger and Hans Burgkmair the Younger, c. 1545–1552)
books.summary: A 169-page illuminated manuscript executed in gouache and watercolour in Augsburg, Germany, documenting miraculous signs, celestial phenomena, and wondrous events from the biblical Flood through 1552. Its three sections cover Old Testament miracles, non-biblical wonders (comets, parhelia, monsters, catastrophes), and scenes from the Book of Revelation. Long lost to scholarship, it resurfaced at auction in 2008 and was published in a scholarly Taschen facsimile in 2013 with a second edition in 2017.

article.fact_check: The tweet attributes the illustration to Heinrich Vogtherr the Younger alone. Scholars identify at least two primary hands on the manuscript — Vogtherr the Younger and Hans Burgkmair the Younger — with possible workshop apprentices contributing additional pages; attribution of specific folios to one hand or the other is not always definitively resolved. The date 'c. 1552' is accurate as a completion date (the final dated wonder is from 17 May 1552), though production spanned roughly 1545–1552.
